claims.assertion: The GPS record shows the trip ran 20.1 km against an optimal 15.5 km (+4.6 km, +30%), so the off-route segment F3 (12:46-13:07) is a real deviation, not measurement noise.
Segment F3 drove 9.70 km where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km of extra distance that no exemption covers, so it is an unexempted off-route segment under RD-1.

No traffic justification exists: F12 records no traffic incidents near the route during the trip window, and the only speed-band facts (F9 Central Expressway 60-69 km/h, F10 PIE 60-69 km/h, F11 Paya Lebar Road 30-39 km/h) show flowing traffic, none of them band 1 or 2, so RD-4 (a) and (b) do not exempt the segment.

There was no rider consent to the reroute: F7 shows no in-app chat messages at all between rider and driver, so no rider message was sent before 12:46 agreeing to the route that produced F3, and the driver's post-trip statement in F8 is not rider consent.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (total $42.52 with distance $28.31 over 20.08 km, F6), so every extra kilometre on the unexempted segment flowed directly into the fare and the refund must be the metered-rate value of that extra distance.

The refund amount is computable from the fare record: unexempted segment extra distance 4.08 km (F3) multiplied by this trip's per-km rate of $1.4099/km (F4: $6.50 per 4.61 km; F6: $28.31 distance fare over 20.08 km) equals $5.75, rounded to the cent.

The driver has 3 upheld route disputes in 90 days (F15), so this case makes the deviation a repeated one and the ruling should carry a flag_account referral for Ryde account review alongside the refund.
The complaint and the driver statement in F8 contain no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, so no SAFE-1 or SAFE-2 escalation is triggered.

weaknesses: The rider has 1 dispute in 90 days with 0 upheld (F14), so the opposing side can argue this account has no record of successful claims - a profile point only, not a defence on the merits.

F1 gives distances but no road names, so the case does not itself tie the optimal route to the PIE; the driver can argue in line with F8 that his GPS exit at Paya Lebar was still the most efficient route, and the +12.2 min duration in F2 as consistent with slower roads.

Segment F3 starts at 12:46 and ends at 13:07, i.e. only at the very end of the trip, so the driver may characterise part of it as the unavoidable final approach into Bedok Mall; F3 does not break the 4.08 km down into named roads for us to rebut with road names, and any km attributed to that approach would fall outside RD-2.

claims.assertion: There is no in-app chat of any kind in this case, so there is no rider message that could amount to route consent before the off-route segment began; the driver's written statement that he simply followed his GPS (F8) is a claim, not consent, and cannot cure the deviation.

The GPS track shows exactly one off-route segment, 12:46–13:07, in which 9.70 km were driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km and straying up to 1720 m from the optimal route (F3); no exemption in RD-3, RD-4 or RD-5 applies to it.

The reroute was not justified by any traffic cause: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window (F12), the expressway and Central Expressway bands in the relevant window were 60–69 km/h (F9, F10), the 30–39 km/h band on Paya Lebar Road (F11) is only a no-incident band on a road the driver chose to enter, and the weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain (F13) — so RD-4 provides no cover for the extra kilometres.

This is a RydeTAXI trip metered by distance (F6: distance fare $28.31 for 20.08 km), with this trip's per-km rate of $1.4099 (F4), so the refund under RD-2 is confined to the unexempt segment's added kilometres: 4.08 km × $1.4099 = $5.75, rounded to the cent, and no time or waiting component is refundable (F6 shows waiting $0.00).

The total excess billed over the optimal route is $6.50 (4.61 km at $1.4099/km, F4), which is larger than the segment figure because it includes sub-0.2 km matching noise and corridor wander that RD-2 expressly leaves unrefunded; only the $5.75 attributable to the single unexempt segment is refundable.

The driver's 90-day record of 5 disputes with 3 upheld, all route-related (F15), makes this an already-established repeated route deviation, so the RD-1 breach in this case should be recorded against the account; the profile is relied on only for that ancillary action, not to establish the deviation itself.

weaknesses: The strongest fact against the driver is F3: a single continuous off-route segment lasting 21 minutes and adding 4.08 km, ending only ~1 minute before drop-off, which is hard to present as inadvertent. RD-1 sets no threshold, so the driver cannot argue the deviation was too small to matter.

The rider's own account (complaint, and F1's 20.1 km vs 15.5 km) matches the GPS record, and RD-2's computation base — the billed excess of $6.50 (F4) — is larger than the $5.75 we concede; the judge may simply award the billed excess.

F8 is a bare assertion with no chat support (F7 shows no messages at all), so the driver cannot show any agreed route; under RD-5 a statement alone is not consent, and G11/G12 offer no fallback for him.

F15 (3 of 5 route disputes upheld in 90 days) invites flag_account under RD-6 and may colour the judge's reading of an otherwise arguable 'GPS chose the route' explanation; A7 lets a driver take the fastest or most efficient route, but the GPS record of +30% distance (F1) and +12.2 min (F2) undercuts 'efficient'.

No traffic excuse is available: F12 records no incidents, so the only fallback would have been the band-4 entry on Paya Lebar Road (F11), which by RD-4(b) is corroborative at best and cannot stand alone.

claims.assertion: The GPS record shows the trip ran 20.1 km against an optimal 15.5 km (+4.6 km, +30%), so the off-route segment F3 (12:46-13:07) is a real deviation, not measurement noise.
Segment F3 drove 9.70 km where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km of extra distance that no exemption covers, so it is an unexempted off-route segment under RD-1.

No traffic justification exists: F12 records no traffic incidents near the route during the trip window, and the only speed-band facts (F9 Central Expressway 60-69 km/h, F10 PIE 60-69 km/h, F11 Paya Lebar Road 30-39 km/h) show flowing traffic, none of them band 1 or 2, so RD-4 (a) and (b) do not exempt the segment.

There was no rider consent to the reroute: F7 shows no in-app chat messages at all between rider and driver, so no rider message was sent before 12:46 agreeing to the route that produced F3, and the driver's post-trip statement in F8 is not rider consent.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (total $42.52 with distance $28.31 over 20.08 km, F6), so every extra kilometre on the unexempted segment flowed directly into the fare and the refund must be the metered-rate value of that extra distance.

The refund amount is computable from the fare record: unexempted segment extra distance 4.08 km (F3) multiplied by this trip's per-km rate of $1.4099/km (F4: $6.50 per 4.61 km; F6: $28.31 distance fare over 20.08 km) equals $5.75, rounded to the cent.

The driver has 3 upheld route disputes in 90 days (F15), so this case makes the deviation a repeated one and the ruling should carry a flag_account referral for Ryde account review alongside the refund.
The complaint and the driver statement in F8 contain no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, so no SAFE-1 or SAFE-2 escalation is triggered.

weaknesses: The rider has 1 dispute in 90 days with 0 upheld (F14), so the opposing side can argue this account has no record of successful claims - a profile point only, not a defence on the merits.

F1 gives distances but no road names, so the case does not itself tie the optimal route to the PIE; the driver can argue in line with F8 that his GPS exit at Paya Lebar was still the most efficient route, and the +12.2 min duration in F2 as consistent with slower roads.

Segment F3 starts at 12:46 and ends at 13:07, i.e. only at the very end of the trip, so the driver may characterise part of it as the unavoidable final approach into Bedok Mall; F3 does not break the 4.08 km down into named roads for us to rebut with road names, and any km attributed to that approach would fall outside RD-2.

claims.assertion: There is no in-app chat of any kind in this case, so there is no rider message that could amount to route consent before the off-route segment began; the driver's written statement that he simply followed his GPS (F8) is a claim, not consent, and cannot cure the deviation.

The GPS track shows exactly one off-route segment, 12:46–13:07, in which 9.70 km were driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km and straying up to 1720 m from the optimal route (F3); no exemption in RD-3, RD-4 or RD-5 applies to it.

The reroute was not justified by any traffic cause: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window (F12), the expressway and Central Expressway bands in the relevant window were 60–69 km/h (F9, F10), the 30–39 km/h band on Paya Lebar Road (F11) is only a no-incident band on a road the driver chose to enter, and the weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain (F13) — so RD-4 provides no cover for the extra kilometres.

This is a RydeTAXI trip metered by distance (F6: distance fare $28.31 for 20.08 km), with this trip's per-km rate of $1.4099 (F4), so the refund under RD-2 is confined to the unexempt segment's added kilometres: 4.08 km × $1.4099 = $5.75, rounded to the cent, and no time or waiting component is refundable (F6 shows waiting $0.00).

The total excess billed over the optimal route is $6.50 (4.61 km at $1.4099/km, F4), which is larger than the segment figure because it includes sub-0.2 km matching noise and corridor wander that RD-2 expressly leaves unrefunded; only the $5.75 attributable to the single unexempt segment is refundable.

The driver's 90-day record of 5 disputes with 3 upheld, all route-related (F15), makes this an already-established repeated route deviation, so the RD-1 breach in this case should be recorded against the account; the profile is relied on only for that ancillary action, not to establish the deviation itself.

weaknesses: The strongest fact against the driver is F3: a single continuous off-route segment lasting 21 minutes and adding 4.08 km, ending only ~1 minute before drop-off, which is hard to present as inadvertent. RD-1 sets no threshold, so the driver cannot argue the deviation was too small to matter.

The rider's own account (complaint, and F1's 20.1 km vs 15.5 km) matches the GPS record, and RD-2's computation base — the billed excess of $6.50 (F4) — is larger than the $5.75 we concede; the judge may simply award the billed excess.

F8 is a bare assertion with no chat support (F7 shows no messages at all), so the driver cannot show any agreed route; under RD-5 a statement alone is not consent, and G11/G12 offer no fallback for him.

F15 (3 of 5 route disputes upheld in 90 days) invites flag_account under RD-6 and may colour the judge's reading of an otherwise arguable 'GPS chose the route' explanation; A7 lets a driver take the fastest or most efficient route, but the GPS record of +30% distance (F1) and +12.2 min (F2) undercuts 'efficient'.

No traffic excuse is available: F12 records no incidents, so the only fallback would have been the band-4 entry on Paya Lebar Road (F11), which by RD-4(b) is corroborative at best and cannot stand alone.

points.response: Accepted and adopted: F7 confirms there is no in-app chat at all, so nothing in the record can be a rider message sent before the 12:46 start of the off-route segment, and F8 is only a post-trip statement (G11 - not consent) - the rider's C4 stands.

Adopted in full: F3 is one continuous unexempted off-route segment, 9.70 km driven against 5.62 km of optimal route, adding 4.08 km - the deviation element of the rider's case (C1-C2) is now common ground.

Adopted: F12 shows no incident near the route, F9/F10 are band-7 (60-69 km/h) and F11 is band 4 (30-39 km/h), none of them the band 1-2 required by RD-4(b), and F13 is fair weather - so RD-4 exempts nothing and the 4.08 km in F3 stays chargeable.

Adopted: F6 shows a RydeTAXI metered fare with distance $28.31 over 20.08 km and waiting $0.00, so under RD-2 the refund is limited to the unexempted segment's extra kilometres at the F4 rate - 4.08 km x $1.4099/km = $5.75, with no time or waiting component.
Accepted for the rider's part - I keep $5.75 as the request rather than the $6.50 in F4, consistent with RD-2 (unexempted segments only; the corridor-200 m and matching difference is not refunded).

Adopted and extended to the ancillary action: F15 shows 3 of 5 route disputes upheld in 90 days, so with this unexempted segment (F3) the case is a repeated breach and should carry flag_account under RD-6 while the profile is used only for that add-on, not for the finding.

Conceded on the arithmetic; F1 and F3 do show a deviation. Our dispute is only its size: RD-1 has no threshold, but RD-2's refund is confined to the unexempt segment's extra_km, which is 4.08 km in F3, not the full billed excess of 4.61 km in F4.
Accepted — F3 is a single 12:46–13:07 off-route segment, 9.70 km against 5.62 km optimal, adding 4.08 km that no exemption in RD-3, RD-4 or RD-5 reaches.

Agreed on the traffic point, and we note F11 cuts against the driver as well: the 30–39 km/h band on Paya Lebar Road is not band 1 or 2, and RD-4(b) would at most corroborate an incident, which F12 shows does not exist.
Accepted; F7 records no in-app messages at all, so nothing was sent before the 12:46 segment start in F3, and the post-trip statement in F8 is a claim, not rider consent under RD-5.

Agreed that this is a metered RydeTAXI trip (F6: distance $28.31 over 20.08 km) so extra kilometres feed the fare, but the metered value to refund is the segment's extra_km only: 4.08 km × $1.4099/km = $5.75 per RD-2, not the billed excess of $6.50 in F4, which also contains sub-0.2 km matching noise and corridor wander RD-2 leaves unrefunded.
No objection to $5.75 — that is exactly the figure in our own brief (D4), and both sides now compute it the same way from F3 and F4.

Accepted only as an ancillary action: F15's 3 upheld route disputes in 90 days makes this a repeated deviation under RD-6, and we do not resist flag_account, but RD-6 is an add-on and cannot be used to inflate the refund beyond the $5.75 computed under RD-2.

Agreed that nothing in the complaint or F8 reads as a threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, so neither SAFE-1 nor SAFE-2 sends this case to a person; the driver also notes the factual record itself contains no such material.

notices.text: We reviewed your RydeTAXI trip and found one stretch of the ride went off the shortest route. The GPS record shows that stretch added 4.08 km to your trip, and nothing explained it — no traffic incident, no road closure, no stop, and no message from you agreeing to a different way. Because your fare is metered, those extra kilometres fed straight into the meter, so we are refunding $5.75 to you as a Ryde voucher. The rest of the higher fare stays, since it comes from general route drift we cannot tie to that stretch. Your account is not affected.

We reviewed a rider complaint about your RydeTAXI trip and found one stretch where the route went off the shortest way, adding 4.08 km against a 15.5 km optimum. Nothing exempted it: no traffic incident or closure was recorded, the weather was fine, there was no stop in that stretch, and the rider never agreed in chat to a different route. Because the meter is distance-based, the rider is being refunded $5.75 as a Ryde voucher. Separately, this is not your first upheld route dispute in the last 90 days, so your account has been referred for review. A reviewer will look at the route history on your trips.
